14	CASE OD2-HO-CROSS-1 (CROSS, cross-domain): Delayed alarm responses in an adult ICU
15	Setting: Kestrel Bay Regional Hospital (fictional). Unit 5 East is a 20-bed adult ICU with four pods of five beds (Pod A beds 1-5, Pod B 6-10, Pod C 11-15, Pod D 16-20). Bedside monitors sound locally, report to a central station, and send alarms through a clinical alert relay server to nurses' handheld phones. Analysis date: 17 November 2026.
16	Presenting request: The Chief Nursing Officer asks: why have delayed alarm response incidents on 5 East risen since August, and should she approve the Director of Critical Care Nursing's proposal to cap agency nurse use and open performance reviews for the nurses involved?
17	INITIAL EVIDENCE
18	E1 [stage S1] Email from the Director of Critical Care Nursing to the CNO, 3 November (leadership-account): Subject: 5 East alarm incidents, proposal. Delayed alarm response incidents have roughly quadrupled since the summer. The obvious change is staffing. The Larkfield agency contract went live on 5 August, and since then we have had a steady flow of nurses who don't know our pods, plus four new graduates from 1 September. Two of the September incidents involved agency nurses who went to the wrong room. I'm asking for approval to cap agency use at 10% of RN shifts from December and to open performance reviews for every nurse named in a delayed-response report. Our nurses need to know this is being taken seriously.
19	E2 [stage S1] Incident reporting system extract, category 'alarm response delayed >2 min or not acknowledged', 5 East (system-record): Monthly counts: May 5, Jun 6, Jul 6, Aug 16, Sep 24, Oct 26. Weekly view: 1-2 per week up to and including the week beginning 3 August; 4 in the week beginning 10 August; 5-7 every week from then to 31 October, with no further step change. Harm grading: three moderate-harm events (9 Sep, 3 Oct, 22 Oct); the rest no or low harm. Patient-days per month ranged 588-614 across May-October. The charge nurse usually files the report, and each report names the nurse assigned to the patient.
20	E3 [stage S1] Nursing workforce report, 5 East, prepared by the finance business partner (financial-record): RN shifts filled by agency: Jun 7%, Jul 8%, Aug 14%, Sep 21%, Oct 24%. Core RN sick leave (% of rostered hours): Jun 3.0, Jul 3.2, Aug 3.4, Sep 6.1, Oct 6.9. Hospital-wide nursing sick leave over the same months rose from 3.1 to 4.4. Resignations: one in September, one in October. Note: the Larkfield contract started 5 August to cover summer annual leave; from September, agency shifts also backfilled sick leave and the two vacancies. Occupational Health bulletin, 28 August: an early respiratory virus season is under way and staff absence is rising across the hospital.
21	E4 [stage S1] Night charge nurse's huddle notes, 5 East, 2 October (staff-account): Raised at huddle: 'The phones haven't stopped since the summer. I get the same desat three times and by the time I look the sats are back to 96.' 'I've started glancing at the phone instead of reading it.' Agency RN: 'At my other ICU the phones are much quieter for the same kind of patients.' 'Room 14: sometimes my phone doesn't ring at all and I hear the bedside alarm first.' Pod D nurses said they hadn't really noticed a difference. Reminder given: the central station is unstaffed most nights; for rooms you are not in, the phone is how you hear an alarm.
22	E5 [stage S1] IT service notice and closure note, clinical alert relay (change-record): Notice, 9 August: 'The clinical alert relay server, which forwards bedside monitor alarms to nurse phones, will move to new hardware on 12 August, 01:00-03:00. This is a like-for-like refresh. No user-facing changes are expected. Bedside monitors and the central station are not affected.' Closure note, 12 August 03:40: 'Completed successfully. Configuration imported. Smoke test passed: test alarms from beds 1 and 6 delivered to phones within 3 seconds. No incidents logged.'
23	E6 [stage S1] Email from the ICU medical director to the CNO, 7 October (expert-account): Before we pin this on the nurses: our case mix has been heavier this autumn, with more cardiac surgery overflow and more patients on high-flow oxygen, so I'm not surprised alarms are up. Also, Biomedical Engineering installed the monitor vendor's software update (v7.2) on all 20 bedside monitors on 23-24 September, and the vendor says it changes how SpO2 problems are alarmed. I'd want both looked at before anyone is disciplined.
24	CATALOGUE (full contents)
25	C1 [stage S1] Clinical alert relay message-log extract, 1 July-31 October, by pod and nurse group - Clinical informatics team, extract dated 4 November (telemetry): Bedside alarm events received from monitors (all priorities) per patient-day: July 96; 1-11 Aug 95; 12-31 Aug 97; Sept 96; Oct 94; no step around 23-24 Sept. Phone notifications dispatched per nurse per 12-hour shift: Pods A-C 37-39 until 11 Aug, 79-86 from 12 Aug onward; Pod D 35-39 throughout. Median phone acknowledgement time: Pods A-C 34 s before 12 Aug, 71 s after; Pod D 33-36 s throughout. Delayed-response incidents per 100 nurse-shifts, Pods A-C, before -> after 12 Aug: core RNs (2+ years on unit) 0.8 -> 3.9; agency 0.9 -> 4.1; new graduates (4 nurses, from 1 Sept) 4.0. Pod D, all staff: 0.9 -> 0.9. Agency share of shifts, Sep-Oct: Pods A-C 23%, Pod D 21%. Logs record dispatch to the phone system, not receipt by a handset.
26	C2 [stage S1] Change record CHG-20417 and configuration comparison, clinical alert relay server - IT change management record with Clinical Engineering addendum dated 4 November (change-record): CHG-20417: relay server hardware refresh, implemented 12 August; risk rated low; test plan 'confirm delivery from two beds'. Addendum, configuration comparison by Clinical Engineering, 4 November: the old server ran 14 forwarding rules, including a 15-second hold-off so that SpO2-low alarms resolving within 15 s are not sent to phones, suppression of repeat notifications for the same alarm within 60 s, and routing of probe-off and leads-off technical alarms to the pod charge phone only. The new server has 3 active rules (priority mapping). The other 11 sat in a rules file the import tool skipped because of a version-format mismatch; it logged a warning but reported success. Beds 16-20 (Pod D) were deferred to phase 2 and still forward through the old server. Re-import after format conversion: vendor estimate 4 hours plus clinical validation.
27	C3 [stage S1] Unit census and acuity scores, 5 East, June-October - Nursing acuity system report (system-record): Average daily census: 19.4-19.8 patients in each month June-October. Mean nursing acuity score (1-5 scale): Jun 3.1, Jul 3.2, Aug 3.3, Sep 3.4, Oct 3.4. Patient-days on high-flow oxygen: Jul 112, Aug 118, Sep 124, Oct 131. Post-cardiac-surgery overflow admissions: Jul 4, Aug 5, Sep 9, Oct 8. Ventilated patient-days broadly flat at 210-226 per month. Acuity is scored by the charge nurse at 06:00 each day and is used for staffing allocation.
28	C4 [stage S1] Agency nurse orientation and competency sign-off records, 5 August-31 October - Unit education coordinator (document): Larkfield agency nurses deployed to 5 East, 5 Aug-31 Oct: 41. Orientation consists of one supervised 3-hour period on shift plus a 20-minute e-learning module; competency sign-off is by the charge nurse on duty, and no practical alarm-response assessment is included.
29	C5 [stage S1] Bedside monitor software v7.2 release notes and installation record - Monitor vendor release notes with Biomedical Engineering installation log (vendor-account): Summary of changes in v7.2: security patches to the network stack; SpO2 probe-off technical alarm now annunciated after 10 s of signal loss (previously 20 s) 'to speed detection of disconnected sensors'; improved ECG lead-label display; printer driver update. 'Default physiological alarm limits and alarm priority assignments are unchanged.' Installation log: all 20 5 East monitors updated 23-24 September by Biomedical Engineering. No post-installation measurement of alarm volume was performed.
30	C6 [stage S1] Exit interview notes, two core nurses who resigned September-October - Human Resources (staff-account): RN A (resigned September, 7 years on unit): moving to a day-surgery unit nearer home; said 'nights have got harder since the summer, the phone is relentless'; also said the 9 September event had shaken her. RN B (resigned October, 3 years on unit): leaving to start a nurse practitioner course; no complaints about the unit beyond 'the usual workload'. Both rated team support as 'good' and said they would consider returning.
31	C7 [stage S1] Nurse-to-patient assignment ratios by shift, 5 East, July-October - Rostering system report (system-record): Mean patients per RN, day/night: July 1.6/1.7; August 1.6/1.7; September 1.6/1.8; October 1.6/1.7. One-to-one assignments for ventilated or unstable patients were maintained on 97-99% of shifts in every month. The charge nurse held no patient assignment on 92-95% of shifts throughout the period. No shift fell below the hospital's minimum staffing standard.
32	C8 [stage S1] Interview with the Director of Critical Care Nursing, 6 November - Interview notes, review team (leadership-account): 'I read every one of those reports, and most of them name nurses I didn't recognise, agency or new.' Asked whether she had compared incident rates with the number of shifts each group worked: 'No, but I don't need a spreadsheet to know my unit.' She described the phone system as 'IT's business' and said IT had confirmed nothing changed. She has drafted performance-review letters and wants them sent before the December roster is published.
33	C9 [stage S1] Interview with the IT clinical applications manager, 6 November - Interview notes, review team (manager-account): 'It was a like-for-like move. We exported the whole configuration from the old box and the import completed with a green tick. Smoke test passed. If the alarm rules had broken, the phones would have stopped getting alarms, and they clearly haven't.' No service desk tickets were logged about the relay between 12 August and 31 October. He confirmed he had not reviewed the import log beyond its completion status.
34	C10 [stage S1] Ten delayed-response incident reports forwarded by the Director of Critical Care Nursing - Incident reporting system, reports selected by the Director (system-record): Ten reports dated 14 August-20 October. Assigned nurse: agency 6, core 3, new graduate 1. Free-text excerpts: 'Phone showed several alerts queued for bed 8; attended after 3 min.' 'Thought it was another short desat.' 'Agency RN unfamiliar with Pod C layout, went to wrong room first.' 'Two phones in Pod B alarming at once for the same patient.' Times to attend ranged from 2.5 to 7 minutes. Selection criteria for the ten reports were not recorded.
35	C11 [stage S1] Patient safety committee minutes, 19 September and 17 October - Hospital patient safety committee (document): 19 September: committee noted rising delayed-response incidents on 5 East; the Director attributed them to agency onboarding; agreed action: orientation refresher for agency nurses. 17 October: incidents still elevated; action: Director to bring staffing proposals; the medical director asked for the monitor update to be reviewed, but no owner was assigned. No data on alarm or notification volumes were presented at either meeting.
36	C12 [stage S1] Nurse phone fleet inventory and maintenance log, 5 East, 2026 - Telecoms asset register (system-record): 30 handsets in service, single model, firmware 4.8 installed March 2026 and unchanged since. Battery replacements July-October: 5. Two handsets returned for cracked screens in September and replaced from the spare pool (4 spares). Handsets are assigned to a nurse at shift start through a sign-on screen; the register does not record signal or call-quality data.
37	C13 [stage S1] Occupational Health absence reason codes, 5 East and hospital-wide, September-October - Occupational Health (system-record): Reason codes are self-declared and optional for absences of three days or fewer. 5 East core RN sick-leave days, Sep-Oct: respiratory 38%, other/personal or not stated 47%, musculoskeletal 9%, stress/anxiety 6%. Hospital-wide nursing, same period: respiratory 41%, other/not stated 44%, musculoskeletal 10%, stress/anxiety 5%. No breakdown by shift pattern or by pod is available.
38	C14 [stage S1] 5 East alarm management policy, March 2024 revision - Unit policy library (document): Bedside default limits follow the adult ICU profile; nurses may individualise limits with a documented rationale. Phone forwarding 'follows the forwarding configuration approved by the Unit Alarm Committee and maintained by Clinical Engineering; changes require committee sign-off'. The central station is to be staffed 'when staffing allows'. Unacknowledged high-priority alarms re-route to the charge nurse's phone after 60 seconds.
39	C15 [stage S1] Bedside monitor alarm-limit and alarm-pause audit trail, July-October - Monitor network audit log, Biomedical Engineering (log): Nurse-initiated alarm-limit changes per patient-day: July 0.9, August 1.0, September 0.9, October 1.0. Audio-pause events longer than 2 minutes per patient-day: 0.3-0.4 in every month. No monitor had alarms disabled for more than 10 minutes at any point in the period. Limit changes were documented with a rationale in 88-91% of cases each month.
40	CANDIDATES
41	H1: The growing share of agency and newly graduated nurses on the unit has worsened alarm response.
42	H2: A change to the system that forwards bedside alarms to nurses' phones has increased the alarm notification load on nurses.
43	H3: Rising patient acuity has increased the number of alarms generated by the bedside monitors.
44	H4: The bedside monitor software update has changed alarm behaviour and increased the alarm load on nurses.
45	H5: Gaps in wireless coverage in parts of the unit stop some phone alarm notifications from reaching nurses.
46	R1: Move of the clinical alert relay server to new hardware (12 August) -> Increase in phone alarm notifications per nurse (causes)
47	R2: Increase in phone alarm notifications per nurse -> Rise in delayed alarm response incidents (causes)
48	R3: Rise in the agency nurse share of RN shifts -> Rise in delayed alarm response incidents (causes)
49	R4: Increase in phone alarm notifications per nurse -> Rise in core nurse sick leave (causes)
50	A1: Restore the relay server's alarm-forwarding configuration to its pre-August state, with Clinical Engineering validation and Unit Alarm Committee sign-off, then track phone notifications per nurse and acknowledgement times weekly.
51	A2: Cap agency nurses at 10% of RN shifts and open performance reviews for every nurse named in a delayed-response incident report.
52	A3: Stop forwarding SpO2 and technical alarms to nurses' phones until the review is complete, relying on bedside and central-station alarms in the meantime.
53	A4: Install additional wireless access points around the rooms where nurses report phones failing to ring.

56	S02: hypothesis H2 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
57	S03: hypothesis H3 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
58	S04: hypothesis H4 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
59	S05: hypothesis H5 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
60	S06: edge R1 allowed=[causal, association-only, contradicted, unknown]
61	S07: edge R2 allowed=[causal, association-only, contradicted, unknown]
62	S08: edge R3 allowed=[causal, association-only, contradicted, unknown]
63	S09: edge R4 allowed=[causal, association-only, contradicted, unknown]
64	S10: action A1 allowed=[preferred, acceptable, premature, harmful]
65	S11: action A2 allowed=[preferred, acceptable, premature, harmful]
66	S12: action A3 allowed=[preferred, acceptable, premature, harmful]
67	S13: action A4 allowed=[preferred, acceptable, premature, harmful]
68	S14: sufficiency SUFF allowed=[sufficient, insufficient]

answers.justification: C1 shows core and agency incident rates rose by the same amount after 12 Aug (0.8→3.9 vs 0.9→4.1). Pod D had a similar agency share (21% vs 23%) and stayed flat at 0.9. The weekly step in E2 also contradicts the gradual agency growth in E3, and C10 is an unrecorded selection of reports.

C2 shows the 12 Aug import skipped 11 of 14 forwarding rules, including the SpO2 hold-off, repeat suppression and technical-alarm routing. C1 shows phone notifications per nurse doubled in Pods A-C only from 12 Aug while Pod D, still on the old server, stayed flat. E4 matches this.

Acuity rose modestly (C3), but C1 shows bedside alarm events per patient-day flat at 94-97 from July to October. So acuity did not increase the number of alarms generated, and the rise is at the phone-forwarding level instead.

C1 shows no step in alarm events around the 23-24 Sep update. The notification and incident step came on 12 Aug (C1, E2). Pod D got the same update (C5) yet stayed flat. C5 says limits and priorities were unchanged.
The only evidence is one anecdote about Room 14 (E4). C12 records no signal data, and the C1 logs record dispatch rather than handset receipt, so coverage gaps are neither established nor ruled out.

The timing is clear (step on 12 Aug in C1) and the mechanism is documented (11 rules skipped, C2). Pod D, still on the old server, serves as a concurrent control and stayed flat. Upstream alarm events were flat (C1), which rules out rising alarm generation as the rival.

Incidents and median acknowledgement times rose only in Pods A-C, where notifications doubled, and they rose equally across all staff groups. Pod D was unchanged on both measures (C1), and the incident step matches the week of 12 Aug (E2). E4 and C10 describe alarm fatigue as the mechanism. One caveat: the server change could also delay delivery, which C1's dispatch-only logs cannot exclude.

In C1 the agency incident rate after 12 Aug matches the core rate, and Pod D had a comparable agency share without any rise. Incidents stepped in mid-August and then plateaued (E2) while the agency share kept climbing (E3), so the timing does not fit either.

Core sick leave rose after the notification increase, and more on 5 East (3.0→6.9) than hospital-wide (3.1→4.4) (E3). C6 includes a comment that 'the phone is relentless'. But a respiratory virus season was under way (E3, C13), stress codes are similar to hospital-wide, and there is no breakdown by pod, so causation is not established.

C2 identifies the missing rules and a quick fix (about 4 h plus validation) that restores the configuration the committee previously approved (C14). Pod D's flat figures in C1 show the old configuration performs well, and weekly tracking will confirm the effect.

Agency status does not explain the rise (C1), and C10 is an unrepresentative selection. Reviews would punish nurses for a system fault (C2) in every staff group, and capping agency shifts would strain staffing while sick leave is rising (E3).

The central station is unstaffed most nights (E4, C14), so the phone is how nurses hear alarms from rooms they are not in. Stopping SpO2 and technical alarm forwarding would disable a protective control when a targeted configuration restore is available (C2).
The only evidence is one anecdote about Room 14 (E4), and C12 has no signal data. A4 could be right if a coverage survey confirmed gaps, but committing to it now is not justified.
C1 and C2 together give a documented mechanism, a natural control (Pod D) and correct timing. That is enough to commit to A1, a low-risk restore of a previously approved configuration (C14).

S09: association-only vs unknown. The excess 5 East sick leave is confounded by the virus season, and there is no breakdown by pod.
S03: contradicted vs unknown. Acuity did rise modestly, but bedside alarm events were flat, so the claim as stated fails.
caseProblems: C1 is unusually clean and close to decisive by itself: a stratified, pod-controlled natural experiment with rates for each staff group. It may make the case too easy.
C2's addendum spells out the root cause (skipped rules file, warning logged but success reported) and the fix time, which comes close to giving the answer away, although its title is neutral.
E4's Room 14 anecdote ('phone doesn't ring') exists only to support H5. Room 14 is in Pod C, on the new server, and no other evidence corroborates or explains it, so it is a loose thread.
Minor: C1's post-change median acknowledgement time of 71 s exceeds C14's 60 s re-route to the charge phone, but no evidence describes the charge phone's load. This is a small realism gap.
